result:
The house does not go silent. That is the first thing I want to correct, because people speak of the night as if it swallows sound, as if the dark is a mouth that closes. It is the opposite. The house speaks more clearly when no one is listening to it.

At 3 AM, the pipes exhale. There is a long, low groan in the walls that sounds like a cello string bowed by a clumsy hand. The radiator ticks in a rhythm that is almost a language—tick, tick, pause, tick—like a clock that has forgotten which direction time flows. The floorboards settle, shifting their load from one joist to the next, and the sound is like a blink.

Outside, a dog barks twice at something no one will ever see. A car door slams three streets away, the echo arriving thin and confused, as if the sound got lost on its way here and arrived apologizing for itself.

And beneath all of it, the refrigerator hums. That small, industrious hum. The house's heartbeat. It has run for eleven years, and it will keep running after I am gone, humming to empty rooms, keeping milk cold for no one, faithful to a purpose that no longer has a person attached to it.

I press my ear to the wall and listen to all of it. The house is not quiet. The house is full. It is full of every sound it has ever swallowed and never finished saying.
